dedupe_keys.name: hong kong redesigning hospital general ward ventilation with computational fluid dynamics to limit cross infection

description: This case study uses computational fluid dynamics to find a simple and cheap ventilation design that reduces cross-infection in hospital general wards. The authors, from the City University of Hong Kong, the Hong Kong Hospital Authority and the Hong Kong Sanatorium and Hospital, simulated and compared how several ventilation systems remove microbes from a ward. Instead of the usual arrangement in which air returns through the corridor, they rearranged the air return so that ventilation is controlled from inside each ward cubicle, together with a higher air change rate. The article was published in the Journal of Hospital Infection in 2011 and is free to read online in PubMed Central under the publisher's COVID-19 free access terms. Coverage is a generic general ward design in Hong Kong. Caveats: the results are simulations without field validation in the article's abstract, and the model files are not published. The simulations show that the rearranged design can markedly improve ventilation performance and microbe removal, matching a properly built isolation room at much lower cost, and that it can be retrofitted in existing wards with far less disruption than a full refurbishment; the authors recommend the parameters for new wards. Simulation uses: ventilation design parameters for infection control and surge capacity planning of hospital wards. Related records: the Flanders care building ventilation audits (case_study-flanders-healthcare-heat-and-ventilation-audits) address ventilation in care buildings elsewhere.
